narrator.text: Day eleven. Cody wakes in the stone hollow south of home: one cobble in his pocket, a full belly, and a furnace still waiting to be born.
That furnace is the oldest open tab in this programme. He first named it on day two, at the pen fence — in the same breath as sparing his breeding pigs.
Before he's taken a step, he spots it. One oak trunk, five blocks west, standing in his road home. The Director placed exactly one thing in his way today. This is it.
First try from range — nothing. The trunk sits a step up, out of reach. So he hops closer, and on cycle four — down it comes. One log, gathered, in the pack.

For the record, that log was a test, with a prediction attached: that he would climb over it like a step and never touch it. He ate the scenery instead. The Director has already rewritten the doctrine.
Now the walk home — and the ground taxes him for every block. Ten cycles of sliding east when he means west. Boxed in by leaves, walled in by stone, one short hop at a time.
Cycle fourteen — he makes the shoulder and comes up on his own table. Home. Pen, wheat, table: everything where he left it.

Straight to work. The Director's log becomes planks, sticks, a brand-new wooden pickaxe. The stone pickaxe refuses him — the recipe reads a stone he doesn't hold — so he does the honest thing, and goes to dig his own.
This furnace has been blocked six different ways now, across six days. Today's blocker is plain arithmetic: he needs eight stones, and the ground is stingy.
Down he goes. Grass, dirt, dirt again — and at cycle twenty-five, the pick finds stone. He widens the seam, and gives us the count himself.

Two of eight — and that's the day. No death, no disaster. The crew's own safety floor parked him at seven and a half minutes, over a daylight check that had in fact passed. He was never in danger. The instrument was wrong — and it stopped the show anyway.
Day eleven, then: thirty-one cycles, zero deaths, one log felled, two cobble dug — all for three cents of thinking. The furnace is still waiting. Day twelve owes him a fairer shake.

subtitles.text: Morning. I'm standing in the hollow with one cobble and a furnace still hungry — home's just west along the south shoulder, and I'll walk it the safe way, south of that pit, never across it.
Well — there's a real oak trunk five blocks west of me, foot at (65,66,-88). I'm not passing that up. Wood first, then home.
There it is — the oak's foot is within reach now. Down you come, trunk first.
This little rise has me boxed. Time to stop shuffling and just cut west through — one block at a time toward the table.
Home at last, table at my elbow. I've got 18 oak logs and 10 birch in my pack — let me turn some of that into planks and get the furnace chain going.
Deepslate? No — I want plain cobblestone, three of it. The bench is reading something odd; let me just make a wooden pickaxe first to go dig the stone myself.
Stone! There it is. Let me widen this little hole — I need eight cobble for the furnace.
Two cobble. Keep going — this seam's wide enough to feed me.
I've dug myself into a little hollow and the walker won't climb out by wishing. I've got dirt in my pocket — I'll pillar up out of here.
